Kaocen flees north and is caught and hanged in Fezzan in 1919.
events.search: Kaocen revolt 1916 1917 Tuareg siege of Agadez Senussi

events.title: The Chemin des Dames and the mutinies, April – June 1917
events.place: The Chemin des Dames ridge, on the Aisne
events.summary: General Nivelle promises to break the German front in two days. On 16 April 1917, French troops attack up the Chemin des Dames ridge, into machine guns that the shelling has left intact. The offensive fails, with over 100,000 French casualties in two weeks. In May and June, soldiers in dozens of divisions refuse to go back to the attack. Pétain replaces Nivelle, gives more leave and better food, waits for the Americans and tanks, and has a few dozen mutineers shot.
events.search: Chemin des Dames Nivelle offensive 1917 French army mutinies

events.title: The Second Battle of the Marne, 15 July – 6 August 1918
events.summary: In the spring of 1918, Germany throws its last forces at the Allied lines and comes back to the Marne. On 15 July it attacks around Reims, but the French are ready. On 18 July, French and American troops led by General Mangin counter-attack from the forest of Villers-Cotterêts with hundreds of tanks. The Germans have to retreat beyond the Vesle. Marshal Foch keeps up the pressure: from now on the Allies advance until the armistice.
events.search: Second Battle of the Marne 1918 Villers-Cotterets counter-attack Foch Chateau-Thierry

events.title: Alsace–Lorraine returns to France, 1918 – 1920
events.summary: Germany had taken Alsace and part of Lorraine from France in 1871. After the armistice, French troops enter Metz on 19 November and Strasbourg on 22 November 1918, to cheering crowds. The Treaty of Versailles returns the land to France on 10 January 1920, and it becomes the departments of Bas-Rhin, Haut-Rhin and Moselle. They keep some of their German-era laws, such as the Concordat on religion, to this day.
events.search: Alsace-Lorraine returns to France 1918 1920 Strasbourg Metz Versailles

events.title: The Battle of Kousséri, 22 April 1900
events.place: On the Chari, near today's N'Djamena
events.summary: Three French columns, one from Algeria across the Sahara, one from Niger and one from the Congo, meet near Lake Chad to fight the warlord Rabih az-Zubayr, who rules the Bornu and the lands south of the lake. At Kousséri, on the Chari, they defeat and kill him; the French commander Major Lamy is killed too. A month later the French found Fort-Lamy, today's N'Djamena, and the military territory of Chad begins.
events.search: Battle of Kousseri 1900 Rabih az-Zubayr Lamy Fort-Lamy conquest of Chad

events.title: Coppolani's "peaceful conquest" of Mauritania, 1902 – 1905
events.place: Trarza, Brakna and Tagant, to Tidjikja
events.summary: North of the Senegal river live the Moorish emirates of Trarza, Brakna, Tagant and Adrar. Xavier Coppolani, a Corsican raised in Algeria who speaks Arabic and knows the Sufi brotherhoods, wins over their emirs and religious leaders one by one, backed by small columns of troops. By 1904 Trarza, Brakna and Tagant have accepted French rule, and France makes Mauritania a territory of its own. Coppolani is killed at Tidjikja in May 1905.
events.search: Xavier Coppolani peaceful conquest Mauritania 1902 1905 Trarza Brakna Tagant Tidjikja

events.title: The Entente Cordiale, 8 April 1904
events.summary: After centuries of rivalry, and only six years after the Fashoda crisis, France and the United Kingdom settle their colonial quarrels. Britain leaves France a free hand in Morocco, and France stops opposing British rule in Egypt. They also share out their claims in Siam, the New Hebrides, West Africa and the Newfoundland fisheries. It is not an alliance, but the two countries draw closer against Germany and fight side by side in 1914.
events.search: Entente Cordiale 1904 France United Kingdom Morocco Egypt

events.title: The Franco-Siamese treaties, 1904 and 1907
events.summary: Siam keeps its independence between British Burma and French Indochina by giving up land. In 1904 it cedes to France Sainyabuli and the land west of the Mekong at Champasak, which go to Laos, and Koh Kong and Mlu Prey, which go to Cambodia. In 1907 it hands over the provinces of Battambang, Siem Reap and Sisophon, which Siam had held since 1795, in exchange for Trat, which French troops had occupied. Cambodia gets back the temples of Angkor.
events.search: Franco-Siamese treaties 1904 1907 Battambang Siem Reap Angkor Sainyabuli Champasak Trat

events.title: The law separating the Churches and the State, 9 December 1905
events.summary: After years of conflict between the Republic and the Catholic Church, Parliament ends the Concordat of 1801. The Republic guarantees freedom of conscience and of worship, but no longer recognises or pays any religion. Church buildings become public property, left for the use of the faithful. The law founds French laïcité. Alsace and Moselle, then German, keep the Concordat to this day.
events.search: 1905 law separation of the Churches and the State laïcité France Concordat

events.title: The Tangier Crisis and the Algeciras Conference, 1905 – 1906
events.summary: On 31 March 1905, Kaiser Wilhelm II lands at Tangier and declares his support for the independence of Morocco, to test the new Entente between France and Britain. War seems possible, and France's foreign minister Delcassé has to resign. At the Algeciras conference in 1906, the powers keep Morocco formally independent but give France and Spain the policing of its ports and a hold on its finances. Britain stands by France, and Germany comes out isolated.
events.search: First Moroccan Crisis Tangier 1905 Wilhelm II Algeciras Conference 1906

events.title: The bombardment of Casablanca, August 1907
events.summary: In July 1907, Moroccans opposed to the French-run works at the port of Casablanca kill nine European workers. On 5 August French warships shell the city and troops land; the city is looted and thousands of Moroccans die. France then occupies the Chaouia plain around Casablanca, as it had occupied Oujda, on the Algerian border, in March. These are the first steps of the French conquest of Morocco.
events.search: Bombardment of Casablanca 1907 Chaouia occupation Oujda

events.title: Gouraud takes the Adrar, 1909
events.summary: After Coppolani's death, the emirate of Adrar and the followers of the religious leader Ma al-Aynayn lead the resistance in the north of Mauritania, with help from Morocco. Colonel Henri Gouraud marches a column across the desert and takes Atar in January 1909, then Chinguetti. The emir of Adrar submits, and by 1912 France has put down the last resistance in the Adrar.
events.search: Gouraud Adrar 1909 Atar Chinguetti Ma al-Aynayn conquest Mauritania

events.title: The conquest of Ouaddai, 1909 – 1911
events.summary: The sultanate of Ouaddai, east of Lake Chad, is the strongest state left in the region, living from the caravan trade across the Sahara. French troops take its capital Abéché in June 1909, but Sultan Dud Murra fights on with the help of the neighbouring sultanates of Dar Masalit and Dar Sila, which kill a French colonel at Doroté in 1910. Dud Murra surrenders in October 1911, and Ouaddai becomes part of French Chad.
events.search: Wadai War Ouaddai 1909 1911 Abeche Dud Murra conquest of Chad

events.title: The Agadir Crisis and the Morocco–Congo Treaty, 1911
events.summary: In May 1911 French troops march into Fez to help the Sultan against a revolt. Germany answers by sending the gunboat Panther to Agadir on 1 July, and Europe fears war. By the treaty of 4 November 1911, Germany accepts that France can make Morocco a protectorate. In return, France cedes to German Kamerun about 275,000 km² of its Equatorial Africa, Neukamerun, and gets a small strip south of Fort-Lamy, the Bec de canard.
events.search: Agadir Crisis 1911 Panther Morocco-Congo Treaty Neukamerun Bec de canard

events.title: The Treaty of Fes and the Fez riots, 1912
events.summary: On 30 March 1912, Sultan Abd al-Hafid signs the Treaty of Fes, making Morocco a French protectorate. Three weeks later, Moroccan soldiers in Fez mutiny, and with the townspeople kill French officers and civilians and attack the Jewish quarter. General Lyautey, the first resident-general, retakes the city and the surrounding region. The Sultan abdicates in August, and in November France gives Spain a zone in the north of Morocco.
events.search: Treaty of Fes 1912 French protectorate Morocco Fez riots Lyautey Abd al-Hafid

events.title: Brazza's treaty with King Makoko, 1880
events.summary: On 10 September 1880 the explorer Pierre Savorgnan de Brazza signs a treaty with Makoko, king of the Teke, who places his lands on the north bank of the Congo under French protection. Brazza founds a post on the river that will become Brazzaville. The French parliament ratifies the treaty in 1882, the start of French Congo.
events.search: Makoko treaty 1880 Brazza Teke Brazzaville French Congo

events.title: The Treaty of Bardo, 1881
events.summary: In April 1881, using raids by Khroumir tribesmen into Algeria as a pretext, French troops enter Tunisia. On 12 May, with soldiers around his palace, Muhammad III as-Sadiq Bey signs the Treaty of Bardo: France takes charge of Tunisia's army and foreign affairs. The 1883 La Marsa Convention completes the protectorate, which lasts until 1956.
events.search: Treaty of Bardo 1881 Tunisia French protectorate Khroumir Sadiq Bey La Marsa

events.title: The Tonkin campaign and the Sino-French War, 1883 – 1885
events.summary: France sends troops to Tonkin, and in August 1883 the Harmand treaty forces the court of Huế to accept a protectorate over Annam and Tonkin. China, which considers Vietnam its tributary, fights back with its armies and the Black Flags. After battles around Lạng Sơn and a French naval campaign off Fuzhou and Taiwan, the Treaty of Tientsin of June 1885 makes China give up its claims.
events.search: Sino-French War 1883 1885 Tonkin campaign Harmand treaty Lang Son Black Flags Tientsin

events.title: The Cần Vương revolt, 1885 – 1896
events.summary: In July 1885 the regent Tôn Thất Thuyết attacks the French garrison of Huế, then flees with the young emperor Hàm Nghi and calls on the Vietnamese to rise to "save the king" (Cần Vương). Scholars lead uprisings across Annam. Hàm Nghi is captured in 1888 and exiled to Algeria, and the last leader, Phan Đình Phùng, dies in 1895; the revolt ends the following year.
events.search: Can Vuong revolt 1885 Ham Nghi Ton That Thuyet Hue Phan Dinh Phung

events.title: The Indochinese Union is founded, 1887
events.summary: On 17 October 1887 France joins the colony of Cochinchina and the protectorates of Cambodia, Annam and Tonkin under one governor-general: the Indochinese Union, or French Indochina. Laos is added in 1899 and Guangzhouwan in 1900. The capital, first Saigon, moves to Hanoi in 1902.
events.search: Indochinese Union 1887 French Indochina governor-general Cochinchina Cambodia Annam Tonkin

events.title: The conquest of Dahomey, 1892 – 1894
events.summary: After a first war in 1890 over the coast around Cotonou and Porto-Novo, Colonel Alfred-Amédée Dodds marches on the kingdom of Dahomey in 1892. King Béhanzin's army, with its women soldiers, is beaten in a series of battles, and Abomey falls in November. Béhanzin surrenders in January 1894 and is exiled to Martinique; Dahomey becomes a French colony.
events.search: Second Franco-Dahomean War 1892 Dodds Behanzin Abomey Dahomey conquest

events.title: The Franco-Siamese crisis, 1893
events.summary: France claims the lands east of the Mekong, held by Siam. After clashes in Laos, French gunboats force their way up the Chao Phraya to Bangkok in July 1893 and blockade the coast. By the treaty of 3 October 1893, Siam gives up all the left bank of the Mekong, which becomes French Laos.
events.search: Franco-Siamese War crisis 1893 Paknam incident Mekong left bank Laos treaty

events.title: The French take Timbuktu, 1893 – 1894
events.summary: In December 1893 a French flotilla on the Niger reaches Timbuktu, the old city of trade and learning, and a column under Colonel Bonnier occupies it. In January 1894 Tuareg fighters wipe out Bonnier's column at Tacoubao. Major Joffre, the future marshal, arrives overland in February and holds the city for French Sudan.
events.search: Timbuktu 1893 1894 French conquest Bonnier Joffre Tuareg Tacoubao

events.title: French West Africa is founded, 1895
events.summary: On 16 June 1895 France places Senegal, French Sudan, French Guinea and Ivory Coast under one governor-general in Saint-Louis: French West Africa. Dahomey joins in 1899, Mauritania, Upper Volta and Niger later. In 1902 the capital moves to Dakar. The federation lasts until 1958.
events.search: French West Africa 1895 AOF founded governor-general Saint-Louis Dakar federation

events.title: The French conquest of Madagascar, 1895 – 1897
events.summary: In 1895 a French expedition lands at Mahajanga and marches inland; thousands of its soldiers die of fever on the way. Antananarivo is shelled and surrenders on 30 September, and the Merina kingdom accepts a protectorate. France annexes Madagascar in August 1896, and after a rising against French rule, General Gallieni exiles Queen Ranavalona III in February 1897 and ends the monarchy.
events.search: Second Franco-Hova War 1895 Madagascar expedition Antananarivo annexation 1896 Gallieni Ranavalona III exile

events.title: The capture of Samori Touré, 1898
events.summary: For almost twenty years Samori Touré, founder of the Wassoulou Empire around Bissandougou, fights the French advance in the upper Niger lands, moving his whole state east into the north of Ivory Coast in the 1890s. Surprised at Guélémou on 29 September 1898, he is captured and exiled to Gabon, where he dies in 1900. His lands are shared between French Guinea, French Sudan and Ivory Coast.
events.search: Samori Toure 1898 captured Guelemou Wassoulou Empire Bissandougou exile Gabon

events.title: The Voulet–Chanoine Mission, 1899
events.summary: Sent from French Sudan to reach Lake Chad, the column of Captains Paul Voulet and Julien Chanoine loots and burns villages across what is now Niger, killing thousands; at Birni-N'Konni in May 1899 most of the town's people are massacred. When Colonel Klobb is sent to take over, Voulet has him shot in July; their own soldiers then kill Voulet and Chanoine. The rest of the column reaches Zinder and Lake Chad.
events.search: Voulet-Chanoine Mission 1899 Birni N'Konni massacre Klobb Niger Zinder

events.title: Nice and Savoy join France, 1860
events.summary: In return for helping Piedmont-Sardinia against Austria in 1859, Napoleon III asks for Savoy and the County of Nice. By the Treaty of Turin of 24 March 1860, King Victor Emmanuel II cedes them, and plebiscites in April approve with huge majorities. France takes over on 14 June 1860. In 1861 the Prince of Monaco also sells Menton and Roquebrune to France.
events.search: Treaty of Turin 1860 Nice Savoy annexation plebiscite Napoleon III Cavour Menton Roquebrune

events.title: The French expedition to Lebanon, 1860 – 1861
events.summary: In 1860 fighting between Druze and Maronite Christians in Mount Lebanon turns into massacres, which spread to Damascus. With the agreement of the other European powers, Napoleon III sends some 6,000 soldiers, who land at Beirut in August 1860 and stay until June 1861. The Ottoman government then makes Mount Lebanon a self-governing district under a Christian governor.
events.search: 1860 Mount Lebanon civil war Druze Maronite massacres Damascus French expedition Beirut Mutasarrifate

events.title: The conquest of Cochinchina and the Treaty of Saigon, 1861 – 1862
events.summary: French and Spanish troops have held Saigon since 1859. In February 1861 they break the Vietnamese lines at Kỳ Hòa, then take Mỹ Tho and Biên Hòa. By the Treaty of Saigon of 5 June 1862, Emperor Tự Đức cedes the three eastern provinces of the south and Côn Sơn island to France, opens ports to trade and allows Catholic missions.
events.search: Cochinchina campaign 1861 1862 Ky Hoa Treaty of Saigon Tu Duc Bien Hoa Gia Dinh Dinh Tuong

events.title: The French intervention in Mexico, 1861 – 1867
events.summary: After Mexico stops paying its foreign debts, France, Britain and Spain land at Veracruz in December 1861. Britain and Spain soon leave, but Napoleon III wants a friendly empire in the Americas. Beaten at Puebla on 5 May 1862, the French take Mexico City in 1863 and make the Austrian archduke Maximilian emperor. Under pressure from the United States and Benito Juárez's republicans, the French leave in 1867, and Maximilian is shot at Querétaro.

events.summary: France declares war on Prussia on 19 July 1870. The German armies win quickly: Napoleon III surrenders at Sedan on 2 September, and two days later the Republic is proclaimed in Paris. Paris is besieged from September and Metz falls in October. On 18 January 1871 the German Empire is proclaimed at Versailles, and Paris surrenders ten days later.
